feedback: If a learner rounds 8,274,500 to 9,000,000 'because the rest is big', have them underline the millions digit and box only the single digit to its right (2); state 'only that one digit decides' and locate the number on a line between 8,000,000 and 9,000,000.

If a learner ranks -7,921 m as deepest because '7 thousand is the smallest number', use a vertical number line with 0 at sea level to show that -9,052 m, the most negative reading, sits furthest below zero, so it is deepest and least in value.

If rounded parts come out the wrong order of magnitude (e.g. reading 214,600 as 21,460), rebuild the period structure (ones, thousands, millions) on a place-value grid and read each number aloud by period before rounding.

To decide whether an estimate is over or under, check each addend: did it round up or down, and by how much? Add up the up-adjustments and the down-adjustments and compare them — the estimate is over when the ups outweigh the downs and under when the downs outweigh the ups. Note that rounding can go in mixed directions: for 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700 to the nearest 100,000, 214,600 rounds down while 388,050 and 96,700 round up, and here the ups slightly outweigh the down, giving a small over-estimate (700,000 vs exact 699,350).
activities.intendedInsight: The same set of numbers can demand different place-value tools — rounding for a headline, exact negatives for a ranking — and estimating first tells you whether the exact answer is believable.
learnerActions: Load a scenario with mixed demands, e.g. three ocean trenches at -8,376 m, -9,052 m and -7,921 m plus a country's population of 8,274,500 needed for a news headline.

For the headline, round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and state the result (8,000,000); name the single digit that decided the rounding (the hundred-thousands digit, 2) and explain why the digits after it do not change the decision.

Order the three trench depths from deepest to shallowest, placing each on a vertical number line with 0 at sea level, and justify ordering by position (more negative = lower = deeper), not by comparing the digits while ignoring the minus sign.

Estimate a combined attendance for three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000, then compute the exact total and state whether your rounded estimate came out over or under, explaining how you can tell.
Say back in context which figure each situation needs: a rounded headline for the population, exact negatives for ranking the trenches.
activities.title: Large-number problem workspace: pick the right tool

feedback: For ordering: the correct deepest-to-shallowest order for -4,000, -10,900, -7,200 is -10,900, -7,200, -4,000, because more negative is lower (further below sea level).
For the estimate: rounding to the nearest 100,000 gives 200,000 + 400,000 + 100,000 = about 700,000; then check the exact total (699,350) is close to it.
For rounding to the nearest million: the deciding digit is the hundred-thousands digit (2), so 8,274,500 rounds down to 8,000,000, not up to 9,000,000.
activities.intendedInsight: Each component place-value skill — rounding to a stated place, ordering negatives by position, estimating by rounding addends — can be executed accurately on its own.
learnerActions: Round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and choose the correct result.
Order three negative trench depths (e.g. -4,000 m, -10,900 m, -7,200 m) from deepest to shallowest.
Estimate a total attendance (e.g. 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700) by rounding each to the nearest 100,000.
